newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-WEAH GETS ONE MATCH BAN, FACES FURTHER ACTION.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-WEAH GETS ONE MATCH BAN, FACES FURTHER ACTION.

text.p: AC Milan striker George Weah was banned for one match on Thursday and could face further suspension for a violent incident at the end of a European Cup match last week.

UEFA, European soccer's governing body, suspended the 30-year-old Liberian for Milan's vital final clash in the Champions' League phase of the European Cup and said it would conduct a full investigation into the incident.

Weah, the world player of the year, is alleged to have attacked Porto defender Jorge Costa in the players' tunnel at the end of a Champions' League match on November 20 and broken his opponent's nose with a head-butt.
Costa underwent surgery last Thursday and is expected to be out of action for at least three weeks.
The Porto defender could also face suspension if UEFA finds he triggered the incident with racial taunts.
Milan officals and Weah's wife Claire claim the Liberian was showered with spit and racial taunts throughout the match and they highlighted his otherwise sparkling record.

"We will give UEFA everything they ask for," said Milan vice-president Adriano Galliani. "For the time being we have sent them a note with the curriculum of Weah, a player who has never had a red card in his life before."
Galliani said the note included declarations from Weah's former clubs Monaco, Paris St Germain and the African soccer federation testifying to the Liberian's fair play.
"George is a loyal man, dedicated to others. I think that in the end this should carry some weight," said Galliani.
Weah himself said little, declaring merely that he was unhappy to miss next week's match.
"I don't want to comment on UEFA's decision, I prefer to wait for the (final) verdict," said Weah.
The decision means that Weah, who is also European and African Player of the Year, will miss Milan's final Champions' League game against Norway's Rosenborg in the San Siro stadium next Wednesday.
Milan need a point to clinch a place in the quarter-finals of the European Cup, a competition they have won five times. If they lose, Rosenborg will qualify instead.
Galliani said Milan "fully accepted" UEFA's decision.
"I think there is a desire to get to the bottom of the affair and understand how an extraordinary man like George Weah could have done this. I think even UEFA have doubts.
"We want to show that even extraordinary personalities such as Weah, if seriously provoked, can react," he said.

UEFA called a telephone-conference meeting of the disciplinary committee to look into the altercation which followed an ill-tempered contest littered with red and yellow cards. The Group D match finished 1-1.

The committee heard reports from Austrian referee Gerd Grabher, the fourth game official Robert Sedlacek and the UEFA match delegate Jim Stjerne Hansen but decided that a more thorough investigation was necessary.
In a break from normal procedure, the committee also heard from the parties involved, including Weah and Milan officials.
"This case is quite a special case," UEFA spokesman Frits Ahlstrom said. "Normally the committee gets an official report and bases its decision on that.
"The clubs get a copy of the report and if they don't like the decision they can appeal. But in this case we have already spoken to all parties."
UEFA decided to expand its investigation into the incident when it was unable to arrange a meeting of all parties because of next Wednesday's Champions' League matches.
No date has been set for the final decision.
